pages.text: By noon, the ice-block seller’s block has shrunk and a pool of water has spread around it. A lump of shea butter left in the sun goes soft and then runny. A kettle on the fire sends up a cloud. Each is a change in the state of matter. Matter exists in three common states: solid, liquid, and gas. A solid keeps its own shape. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. A gas spreads out to fill any space. The same material, such as water, can exist in all three.

pages.alt: A large block of ice melting on a market table, a lump of shea butter softening in the sun, and a kettle giving off a cloud.

pages.text: All matter is made of tiny particles. In a solid they are packed closely in fixed positions and can only vibrate. In a liquid they are still close together but can slide past each other. In a gas they are far apart and move quickly in all directions. Heating gives particles more energy. Heat a solid enough and it melts into a liquid. Heat the liquid and it evaporates or boils into a gas. Cooling reverses the changes: a gas condenses into a liquid, and a liquid freezes into a solid. Pure water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.

Cooling reverses the changes: a gas condenses into a liquid, and a liquid freezes into a solid.
Pure water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.
pages.alt: Three boxes showing particles packed tightly in a solid, close but disordered in a liquid, and far apart in a gas, with arrows labelled melting, boiling, condensing, and freezing.

pages.text: Rock seems to be the most solid thing there is. But deep inside the Earth it is extremely hot. At temperatures of around 1,000 °C, rock melts into a thick, glowing liquid called magma. Where magma forces its way to the surface, we have a volcano. Once it flows out, it is called lava. As lava cools, it freezes back into solid rock. Rocks formed this way are called igneous rocks. Granite, which builders across Ghana crush into chippings, formed from magma that cooled slowly underground long ago.

As lava cools, it freezes back into solid rock.
Rocks formed this way are called igneous rocks.
Granite, which builders across Ghana crush into chippings, formed from magma that cooled slowly underground long ago.
pages.alt: A cutaway of a volcano showing glowing magma rising from deep underground and lava flowing down the outside.

pages.text: Temperature is not the whole story. Pressure also affects changes of state. In a pressure cooker, the high pressure keeps water liquid well above 100 °C, so beans cook faster. Inside the Earth, the enormous weight of the rock above squeezes hot rock so hard that much of it stays solid, even though it is hot enough to melt. If that pressure is reduced, some of the rock can melt without getting any hotter. Now imagine a volcano buried under a sheet of ice hundreds of metres thick. The ice is part of the weight pressing down.

pages.alt: A pressure cooker on a stove beside a cross-section of the Earth’s crust with a thick ice sheet on top and arrows showing its weight pressing down.

pages.text: Iceland, an island in the far north, has many volcanoes under glaciers. In April 2010, one of them erupted through its ice cap. The melted ice caused floods, and a cloud of ash stopped aeroplanes flying across Europe for days. Scientists have found that when Iceland’s thick ice melted at the end of the last ice age, about 12,000 years ago, eruptions became many times more frequent. With less pressure on the rock below, more rock melted. Glaciers are shrinking again today because of global warming. Researchers are studying whether this will cause more eruptions in future. No single eruption has yet been proved to result from it.

pages.text: Ghana has no active volcanoes. The nearest is Mount Cameroon. But changes of state shape our lives all the same. Water evaporates from the sea and the Volta Lake, condenses into clouds, and falls as rain. And melting ice far away affects our coast. Gases such as carbon dioxide, released when we burn fuels and forests, trap heat in the atmosphere. This is the greenhouse effect. As the world warms, ice on land melts and seawater expands, so the sea level rises. At Keta and Ada, the sea is already taking land and homes.

activities.question: How are the particles arranged in a liquid?
options: Far apart and moving quickly in all directions
Close together but able to slide past each other
Packed in fixed positions, only vibrating

activities.question: What is the difference between magma and lava?
options: Magma is found only in the sea
Magma is solid and lava is liquid
Magma is molten rock underground; lava has reached the surface

activities.question: Why can very hot rock deep in the Earth remain solid?
options: It is too far from the Sun to melt
The great pressure of the rock above keeps it solid

activities.question: Apply it: A cold bottle of water taken from a fridge becomes wet on the outside. Which change of state explains this?
options: Water vapour in the air condenses on the cold surface
Water leaks through the plastic by melting
The water inside evaporates through the bottle

activities.prompt: Arrange the steps by which melting ice could lead to an eruption.
items: Greenhouse gases trap more heat in the atmosphere.
A glacier lying over a volcano melts and becomes thinner.
The weight pressing down on the rock below is reduced.
With less pressure, more hot rock melts into magma.
Magma rises to the surface, and the volcano erupts.
